screens.title: Collision Detection and Triggers
screens.subtitle: How colliders, triggers, and event callbacks let your game objects detect and respond to interactions

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how Unity detects when objects touch, pass through, or remain near one another. Colliders are the invisible shapes the physics engine uses to see objects; they are the skin, not necessarily the visual mesh. You will see how primitive colliders like boxes and spheres trade accuracy for performance, when a mesh collider is appropriate, and how the Is Trigger setting changes a collider from a physical boundary into a detection zone. We also cover the six primary C# callbacks used for collisions and triggers, and the rule that at least one interacting object needs a Rigidbody for events to fire. Finally, we'll explore Physics Layers and the Layer Collision Matrix so you can limit which objects check against each other. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the right collider type, implement the correct event methods, and optimize interactions with layers. Think about a pickup that should not block the player: what collider setup would let it detect entry but not stop motion?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Colliders form the physical boundaries and detection zones; triggers detect passage without blocking; at least one Rigidbody is required for events to be sent.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide your practice and code. First, you'll be able to explain what Collider components do and list common types so you can choose appropriate shapes. Knowing the purpose and trade-offs of Box, Sphere, Capsule, and Mesh Colliders helps you balance accuracy and performance. Second, you will distinguish physical colliders from triggers and decide when to use each—triggers detect entry without blocking motion, while solid colliders produce physical responses. Third, you'll write C# event handlers to respond to collisions and triggers: the OnCollision and OnTrigger method families deliver the information your script needs. Finally, you will use Physics Layers and the Layer Collision Matrix to limit checks and optimize performance. Each objective includes a quick mnemonic or visual so you remember the role of the collider as the physics skin and the trigger as a detection zone. As you practice, aim to pick the simplest collider that fits the gameplay need; complexity costs C P U time.

screens.title: What is a Collider?
screens.subtitle: The physics 'skin' that defines an object's physical bounds

narration.text: A Collider is a component that defines the physical shape Unity uses for collision detection. Think of it as a visible object's invisible skin that the physics engine checks for contact and overlap. Colliders do not have to match the visual mesh exactly; often a simpler shape is better for performance. A concrete example: a crate may use a Box Collider even if its model has beveled edges because the box shape is cheaper to test and behaves predictably for blocking movement. A common misconception is to assume colliders are optional for all visible objects; they are required when you expect physical interaction, and at least one interacting object must also have a Rigidbody to send events. Another confusion is treating a Mesh Collider as always superior — while it can be more accurate, mesh colliders are expensive and can cause problems for dynamic objects unless configured as convex. Remember the rule: use the simplest collider that fulfills the gameplay need. Question for reflection: when would you accept less accuracy for better performance in your scene? What is a Collider? means colliders are the physics shapes unity uses for collisions; choose simplicity and performance over exact mesh fidelity when possible.. In practical terms, the physics 'skin' that defines an object's physical bounds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Primitive Colliders: Box, Sphere, Capsule
screens.subtitle: Efficient shapes for common game objects and characters

narration.text: Unity provides several primitive colliders that are fast and stable for runtime physics. A Box Collider represents a cube or rectangular prism and is ideal for crates, floors, or walls. A Sphere Collider fits a spherical volume and is efficient for round projectiles or simple pickups. A Capsule Collider is a cylinder with rounded ends and is the usual choice for characters because it allows smooth movement over small bumps. Concrete example: a player character typically uses a Capsule Collider so steps and slopes do not catch on sharp corners. A common misconception is that the most accurate shape is always best; in practice a Sphere Collider may simplify collision responses and avoid small jitter when compared to a tightly-fitting mesh. Use these primitives when you need stable, inexpensive collision checks. Practice combining primitives to approximate complex geometry instead of relying on an exact mesh collider for moving objects. Primitive Colliders: Box, Sphere, Capsule means use box, sphere, and capsule colliders for predictable, high-performance collision checks; combine them to approximate complex shapes.. In practical terms, efficient shapes for common game objects and characters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 03 › Chapter 3.2 › Primitive Colliders
Primitive collider types
Box Collider: Efficient for rectangular objects like crates, floors, and walls.
Sphere Collider: Best for rounds and projectiles; simple overlap checks.
Capsule Collider: Common for characters to allow smooth movement over bumps.
Example: Player uses a Capsule Collider so stepping over small obstacles does not produce snagging.
Practical patterns
  • Combine boxes to approximate a table or complex crate instead of a mesh collider.
  • Spheres simplify contact math and can reduce jitter for fast-moving objects.
  • Capsules are forgiving on slopes and are stable for continuous character movement.
Common mistake: tightly fitting a primitive to every detail. Overfitting increases checks for little gameplay benefit.

screens.title: Mesh Collider and Is Convex
screens.subtitle: When to use full mesh geometry and the convex trade-off

narration.text: A Mesh Collider gives you collision based on the actual mesh geometry of a model. This provides the most accurate contact shape but at a cost: detailed meshes are expensive to test, and non-convex mesh colliders cannot be used with dynamic rigidbodies in the same way as primitives. For dynamic objects you can enable Is Convex, which simplifies the collider to a convex hull so the physics engine can simulate it safely; the trade-off is lost geometric detail. A concrete example: use a Mesh Collider for a static level prop like a complex stone arch, because it doesn't move and accuracy matters for player navigation. A common misconception is to assign mesh colliders to every moving object to be 'exact' — that often leads to performance problems and unstable physics. Instead, prefer primitive combinations for dynamic objects and reserve mesh colliders for static geometry. Final takeaway: reserve mesh colliders for static, complex shapes, and use convex only when dynamic accuracy is worth the simplification. Module 03 › Chapter 3.2 › Mesh Collider
Mesh Collider (detailed)
Accurate collision using the model's geometry. Best for static level pieces where visual accuracy matters and the object does not move.
When to use
Rocks, complex architecture, or props that remain static in the scene.
Is Convex option
Convex simplifies the mesh to a convex hull which is safe for dynamic rigidbodies but loses concave detail. Use when you need a moving object's mesh-based collision but can accept simplification.
Mistake: Using non-convex mesh colliders on moving objects can produce errors or be unsupported by the physics engine.
Practical recommendation
For dynamic objects approximate complex shape with multiple primitive colliders. Reserve mesh colliders for static scene geometry and enable Is Convex only when dynamic behavior requires mesh-based approximation.

screens.title: Collider vs Trigger — Choosing the right mode
screens.subtitle: When to block motion and when to detect it without collision response

narration.text: The crucial difference between a collider used as a solid and a collider used as a trigger comes down to whether you want physical interaction or pure detection. With Is Trigger unchecked, two colliders that meet will generate physical contact: forces, bouncing, and collision callbacks like OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit. When Is Trigger is checked, the collider stops acting as a solid boundary and becomes a detection zone that objects can pass through; the engine emits OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit instead. A practical example is a speed boost pad: mark its collider as a trigger so the car passes through while you apply a temporary force on entry. A common misconception is that triggers do not require Rigidbody involvement — they still do: at least one of the interacting objects must have a Rigidbody for the engine to dispatch events. Another misunderstanding is to use triggers for blocking behavior; triggers will not prevent movement. Closing question: in your game, which areas should remain solid and which should be triggers to support gameplay flow? Collider vs Trigger — Choosing the right mode means use solid colliders for blocking and physics responses, and triggers for detection zones where objects should pass freely.. content.html:
Module 03 › Chapter 3.2 › Collider vs Trigger
Solid Collider (Is Trigger unchecked)
Produces physical contact. Unity sends OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, OnCollisionExit to appropriate scripts. Use for walls, floors, and objects that should block or push.
Mistake: Expecting a trigger to stop movement. Triggers do not block; they only detect.
Trigger (Is Trigger checked)
Becomes a detection volume. Unity sends OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, OnTriggerExit. Use for pickups, detection zones, damage fields, and entering areas that should not impede motion.
Example: Speed boost pad should be a trigger to avoid physically impeding the vehicle.
Remember: triggers still require a Rigidbody on at least one interacting object to receive event callbacks.

screens.title: OnCollisionEnter / Stay / Exit
screens.subtitle: Handling physical collision events in C#

narration.text: The OnCollision family of methods receives a Collision object that contains rich information about the contact. OnCollisionEnter fires when contact begins, OnCollisionStay runs while the colliders remain in contact, and OnCollisionExit runs when contact ends. The Collision parameter gives you the other GameObject, the Contacts array, and the relative velocity so you can make decisions based on impact strength or contact points. For example, in the provided PlayerInteraction script you can detect an Enemy tag via CompareTag and then reduce health or play a sound when OnCollisionEnter occurs. A frequent mistake is using equality checks on names instead of CompareTag; CompareTag avoids allocations and runs faster. When only one object has a Rigidbody, Unity will route collision events to the Rigidbody's GameObject. Concrete example: if your player cube has a Rigidbody and it collides with a static environment collider, OnCollisionEnter on the Player will receive a Collision object describing that hit. Close by thinking about what contact details you need: contact normal, relative velocity, or specific collider reference — these determine your response logic. OnCollisionEnter / Stay / Exit means use oncollisionenter/stay/exit with the collision parameter to respond to physical impacts; use comparetag for efficient checks.. content.html:
Module 03 › Chapter 3.2 › OnCollisionEnter / Stay / Exit
Code excerpt (visual)
// Inside PlayerInteraction
void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
{
    Debug.Log("Collided with: " + collision.gameObject.name);
    if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Enemy"))
    {
        Debug.Log("Player hit an enemy!");
        // e.g., take damage, play sound
    }
}

void OnCollisionStay(Collision collision) { /* ... */ }

void OnCollisionExit(Collision collision)
{
    Debug.Log("Stopped colliding with: " + collision.gameObject.name);
}
Explanation
  • The Collision parameter includes gameObject, collider, contacts, and relativeVelocity.
  • Use CompareTag to check for categories such as "Enemy" instead of string equality with name.
  • Events go to the Rigidbody owner when only one object has a Rigidbody.
Example scenario: Player collides with an enemy capsule, detect collision in OnCollisionEnter and apply damage based on relativeVelocity.
Check: did you remember to add a Rigidbody to at least one interacting object? If not, no collision events will fire.

screens.title: OnTriggerEnter / Stay / Exit
screens.subtitle: Detecting entry, presence, and exit from detection volumes

narration.text: Trigger callbacks use a simpler Collider parameter and are used when Is Trigger is checked. OnTriggerEnter runs when another collider enters the trigger volume, OnTriggerStay while it remains, and OnTriggerExit when it leaves. The Collider parameter references the other object's Collider component and through it you can access gameObject and tag metadata. A concrete example from the lab: the Pickup sphere is a trigger; when the player enters the sphere OnTriggerEnter checks CompareTag("Pickup"), logs pickup activity, and destroys the pickup. Be careful: triggers still require at least one Rigidbody on the interacting objects for events to be sent. Another common error is attempting to use OnTrigger methods with 2D colliders and 3D colliders mixed together — they are separate systems and will not communicate. For gameplay design, triggers are your detection tools for pickups, damage zones, level boundaries, and any area where you want to respond without stopping motion. What small piece of feedback should you provide players when they enter a trigger in your game? OnTriggerEnter / Stay / Exit means use ontriggerenter/stay/exit to detect presence in detection zones; the collider parameter provides access to the entering object.. In practical terms, detecting entry, presence, and exit from detection volumes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trigger callbacks

content.html:
Module 03 › Chapter 3.2 › OnTriggerEnter / Stay / Exit
Trigger code (visual)
void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
{
    Debug.Log("Entered trigger: " + other.gameObject.name);
    if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Pickup"))
    {
        Debug.Log("Player picked up an item!");
        Destroy(other.gameObject);
    }
}

void OnTriggerStay(Collider other) { /* ... */ }

void OnTriggerExit(Collider other) { /* ... */ }
Key points
  • Collider parameter is simpler than Collision and points to the other collider.
  • Best for pickups, area triggers, and non-blocking detection.
  • Remember Rigidbody requirement: at least one interacting object must have a Rigidbody.
Lab example: Pickup sphere destroys itself when the player enters its trigger, giving immediate feedback in the Console.

screens.title: Rigidbodies and Event Routing
screens.subtitle: Which GameObject receives collision or trigger events and why

narration.text: Event routing depends on where Rigidbody components live. Unity only dispatches collision or trigger callbacks when at least one of the interacting objects has a Rigidbody. If two colliders without rigidbodies overlap, physics events are ignored by the engine. If one object has a Rigidbody and the other does not, collision events will be sent to the Rigidbody's GameObject. If both objects have Rigidbodies, both will receive appropriate events. Consider a static environment collider and a dynamic player with a Rigidbody: the Player will receive OnCollisionEnter when it hits the environment. This routing matters for script placement: attach your interaction handling script to the Rigidbody-bearing object when only one side moves. A common confusion is expecting both objects to always receive events; that only happens if both have Rigidbodies. Concrete example: in the lab, the Player cube has a Rigidbody and receives OnTriggerEnter when moving through the Pickup sphere. Reflect: where should you attach damage-handling logic so it consistently receives collision callbacks in your systems? Rigidbodies and Event Routing means at least one rigidbody is required; events go to the rigidbody's gameobject when only one object is dynamic.. In practical terms, which gameobject receives collision or trigger events and why. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event routing
keyIdea.text: At least one Rigidbody is required; events go to the Rigidbody's GameObject when only one object is dynamic.

content.html:
Module 03 › Chapter 3.2 › Rigidbodies & Event Routing
Rules for events
  • No Rigidbody on either object → physics events are not sent.
  • One Rigidbody → events sent to the Rigidbody's GameObject.
  • Both Rigidbodies → both GameObjects receive events.
Design tip: attach interaction scripts to the object that owns the Rigidbody for predictable callbacks.
Example scenario
Player cube has a Rigidbody, environment colliders do not. When the Player hits an enemy or pickup, the Player receives the event methods and its script can react accordingly.
Misconception: Adding a Rigidbody to everything is not always needed and can increase simulation cost; add them where dynamic motion or event routing requires it.

screens.title: Physics Layers and the Layer Collision Matrix
screens.subtitle: Controlling which objects check collisions to optimize performance

narration.text: Physics Layers let you assign GameObjects to categories and the Layer Collision Matrix in Project Settings controls which categories interact. By default every object is on the Default layer and collides with everything, which is often unnecessary. A practical workflow is to add layers such as PlayerLayer, EnemyLayer, and PickupLayer, assign GameObjects accordingly, and then open Edit, Project Settings, Physics to modify the Layer Collision Matrix. Uncheck boxes to prevent pairs of layers from colliding. For example, you might prevent EnemyLayer from colliding with EnemyLayer to stop enemies from pushing each other, or prevent PlayerLayer from colliding with PickupLayer if pickups should be triggers only. This reduces the number of collision checks and improves performance. A common error is to assume the matrix affects triggers differently — it still governs whether physics checks occur, so set layers thoughtfully. Try an experiment: disable Player-Enemy collisions in the matrix and observe that the Player no longer physically collides with enemies even if both have colliders; your scripts can still detect and respond if triggers or event routing remains appropriate. Physics Layers and the Layer Collision Matrix means use layers and the layer collision matrix to disable unnecessary collision checks and improve physics performance.. In practical terms, controlling which objects check collisions to optimize performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Here are three compact ideas to remember going forward. First, a Collider defines a GameObject's physical shape for the physics engine; it is separate from the visual mesh and should be as simple as the gameplay allows. Second, primitive colliders — Box, Sphere, and Capsule — are efficient and usually the best choice for dynamic objects. Third, Mesh Colliders provide geometric accuracy for static geometry but are costly and require Is Convex for many dynamic scenarios. Keep these points in mind when choosing colliders so your game remains both accurate and performant. As you work in the lab, ask yourself whether each collider improves gameplay enough to justify its cost. narration.text: Three additional concepts to keep in mind: first, triggers detect entry without blocking motion — use them for pickups, damage zones, and sensors. Second, the OnCollision and OnTrigger method families deliver the necessary data: Collision includes contacts and relative velocity, Collider gives a handle to the other collider. Use CompareTag rather than name checks for performant, reliable identification. Third, Physics Layers and the Layer Collision Matrix let you disable unnecessary checks to improve performance; assign sensible layers like PlayerLayer, EnemyLayer, and PickupLayer and uncheck interactions that are not needed.
